在此订阅：Apple 播客 | Spotify |除了 Nvidia 与黄仁勋丑闻的淫秽细节之外，还有一个关于国家安全和推动人工智能繁荣的先进芯片的故事。但这些芯片到底是什么？它们为何如此重要？本·布坎南 (Ben Buchanan) 是拜登总统的人工智能顾问之一，他在与黄这样的人交谈时帮助制定了美国的一些芯片控制政策。在本期《银河大脑》中，他详细分析了这些芯片为何如此有价值，以及它们为何对中美关系和人工智能的未来产生如此大的影响。以下是该集的文字记录： Ben Buchanan：我们与 Jensen 和 Nvidia 进行了很多对话。他们谈论的是技术，而不是间谍或性或类似的东西。所以这是它的一个新维度。但从技术角度来看，这实际上与我们在拜登政府中的担忧非常一致。 [音乐]查理·沃泽尔：我们从英伟达-黄仁勋丑闻中走得越远，就越清楚地看到，尽管有所有淫秽的细节，但这个故事的内涵远比表面上看到的要多得多。是的，这是一起所谓的中国间谍性丑闻。这是科技巨头的陨落。这是一个巨大的硅谷宫廷阴谋故事。但随着时间的推移，这个故事的中心似乎是在华盛顿特区。英伟达与黄仁勋事件本质上是一场地缘政治惊悚片。
这是中美之间关于先进人工智能芯片和人工智能竞赛的冷战引发的一系列连锁事件。因此，要真正理解为什么黄仁勋必须辞职，为什么他被传唤到国会作证，为什么美国证券交易委员会据报道对英伟达发起调查，你必须了解美国是如何陷入与中国的人工智能竞赛中的，以及英伟达的芯片如何推动人工智能的繁荣。你必须了解导致英伟达销售的芯片受到出口限制的政策，以及英伟达和黄爱丽据称利用的复杂漏洞将芯片带入中国。今天我的客人：他不仅理解这个故事的每一个元素；他还理解这个故事的每一个细节。他帮助塑造它。本·布坎南 (Ben Buchanan) 是拜登政府期间的前白宫人工智能特别顾问。布坎南帮助设计了针对中国的芯片出口管制措施，黄仁勋和英伟达曾游说反对这一措施。他与坦图姆·柯林斯 (Tantum Collins) 共同撰写了这本新书《痛苦的斗争：超级智能、超级大国和世界的命运》。他参与了许多事件，导致了我们现在的处境。今天，他将帮助我们这些凡人真正了解中国、芯片、黄仁勋、人工智能竞赛到底发生了什么，以及最重要的是，为什么这一切都很重要。他现在加入我。我是查理·沃泽尔，这是银河大脑。 [音乐] 沃泽尔：本·布坎南，欢迎来到银河大脑。本·布坎南：谢谢你邀请我。
沃泽尔：所以我希望在这次采访中我们可以提出一些非常基本的问题，这些问题将有助于我们更深入地了解中美竞争、实验室；发生了什么事。但首先我想问一下黄仁勋的情况。您是否根据我们现在所知的情况重新审视了您与他或他的公司的互动？比如，现在回想起来，是否有一些事情看起来像是脆弱的迹象？考虑到您与整个故事的关系，您如何看待这个新闻时刻？布坎南：就背景而言，我是白宫特别顾问

【原文 English Original】
Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube Beyond the salacious details of the Nvidia–Jensen Huang scandal is a story about national security and the advanced chips powering the AI boom. But what exactly are these chips, and why do they matter? Ben Buchanan was one of President Biden’s AI advisers and helped write some of the U.S. policies on chip controls, in conversation with people like Huang. In this episode of Galaxy Brain , he breaks down what makes those chips so valuable and why they have such implications for the U.S.-Chinese relationship and the future of AI. The following is a transcript of the episode: Ben Buchanan: We had a lot of conversations with Jensen and with Nvidia. They were conversations about technology, not spies or sex or anything like that. So that’s a new dimension to it. But from a technology perspective, this is actually remarkably consistent with the concerns that we had in the Biden administration. [ Music ] Charlie Warzel: The further we get out from the Nvidia–Jensen Huang scandal, the more it seems clear that, despite all the salacious details, there’s a lot more to this story than meets the eye. It’s an alleged Chinese-spy sex scandal, yes. It’s the fall of a tech giant. It’s this huge, Silicon Valley palace-intrigue story. But as time goes by, it seems that the epicenter of this story is in Washington, D.C. The Nvidia–Jensen Huang affair is, at heart, a geopolitical thriller. It is a series of cascading events that’s been set in motion by a cold war between China and the United States over advanced AI chips and the AI race. And so to really understand why Huang had to resign, why he’s being called before Congress to testify, why the SEC has reportedly launched a probe into Nvidia—you have to understand how the U.S. got locked in this AI race with China, and how Nvidia’s chips work to power the AI boom. You have to understand the policies that have led to the export restrictions on the chips that Nvidia sells, and the convoluted loopholes that Nvidia and Alice Huang have allegedly used to get chips into China. And my guest today: He not only understands every element of this story; he helps shape it. Ben Buchanan is the former White House special adviser on AI during the Biden administration. Buchanan helped design the chip-export controls on China that Huang and Nvidia lobbied against. And along with Tantum Collins, he’s the author of this new book, The Bitter Struggle: Superintelligence, Superpowers, and the Fate of the World . He was in the room for so many of the events that led to where we are now. And today, he’s going to help us mere mortals actually understand what the heck is going on with China, chips, Jensen Huang, the AI race, and crucially, why all of it matters. He joins me now. I’m Charlie Warzel, and this is Galaxy Brain . [ Music ] Warzel: Ben Buchanan, welcome to Galaxy Brain . Ben Buchanan: Thanks for having me. Warzel: So I’m hoping in this interview that we could do some very basic questions that will lead to this deeper understanding of the U.S.-China race, the labs; what’s going on. But first I just want to ask about Jensen Huang. Have you taken what we know now and reexamined any of either the interactions you’ve had with him or his company? Like, were there things in retrospect that now that look like signs of vulnerability? How are you processing this news moment, given your relationship to this entire story? Buchanan: For background, I was the White House special adviser for AI and worked in the National Security Council, and was the architect of a lot of the chip controls that seem to be at the crux of this story here. In the course of doing that work for four years, we had a lot of conversations with Jensen and with Nvidia. They were conversations about technology, not spies or sex or anything like that. So that’s a new dimension to it. But from a technology perspective, this is actually remarkably consistent with the concerns that we had in the Biden administration. Certainly about the importance of chips to national security, the importance of AI to national security, and the necessity to cut off smuggling routes and remote access routes for China to get access to that technology. So, in some sense, it’s like a new chapter in a long-running novel. Maybe a particularly salacious and interesting chapter. But it fits the themes of the novel that I’ve lived, I guess now for six years. Warzel: Some of this stuff, especially. And I want to get into the stuff about Megaspeed: the company that Huang’s alleged mistress, and alleged Chinese intelligence asset, worked for. That’s in your book. Megaspeed is in your book. And so I’m just curious. Like, was all this on your radar, and you were expecting it all to come out in some fashion? Or were you pretty shocked by the fact that we’re all talking about this right now? Buchanan: I never knew of the sex thing. As best I can recall, I did not know of Megaspeed in the government. I definitely don’t think I ever heard the name Alice Huang. Megaspeed is in the book because The New York Times did a good story on it 13 or 14 months ago. And it looked to us, when we were writing the book, as a great avatar or example of exactly the kind of smuggling and remote access we were worried about, and we were trying to prevent. While the particulars of this case are new to me, or at least were not something we discussed in the government, the general idea of circumvention of the export controls because this technology is so important was something that we spent a lot of time on and in fact were actively trying to combat. Warzel: So I wanna ask some basic questions here, because I imagine I’m not alone in what is essentially like a pretty shallow understanding of the story in Nvidia. I think, you know, reading the news, a lot of people understand they make advanced AI chips, power the boom we’re experiencing here. They have an extraordinary amount of market share. But walk me through just to set the table here. Like, why is that? What makes Nvidia’s chips so great, so necessary, such a fundamental part of this whole boom? Buchanan: I would look at Nvidia as a key part of maybe the world’s most advanced supply chain and manufacturing process. So Nvidia designs the chips that are incredibly intricate—hundreds of billions of transistors at nanometer scale—that enable this AI revolution that we’re part of, for better or for worse. And those chips are made in Taiwan almost exclusively at TSMC using equipment from ASML in the Netherlands. These are three companies we profile in a lot of detail in the book, because they’re three of the most important companies in the world. Everyone knows of Nvidia; some people know of TSMC; almost no one knows of ASML. But it’s that kind of supply chain, and then all their subcontractors from there, that is at the core of AI. In AI, we have this notion called the bitter lesson , which is the inspiration for the book’s title, The Bitter Struggle . And the bitter lesson is that AI scientists want to make AI systems almost in this divine-creation process, in which they’re handcrafting the algorithms to perfectly mimic or encapsulate human knowledge. But actually, what works much better, we’ve observed, is giving the systems a flexible algorithm from which to learn. A lot of computing power. And getting out of the way. And that’s why it’s computing power—and in particular these days, Nvidia’s chips—that are at the absolute forefront of this AI story, and therefore this geopolitical story. Because what companies have realized is they can scale up the amount of computing power. They can scale up the amount of Nvidia chips that are used to make AI systems, and they get much more powerful systems as a result. In a very predictable fashion. And that, more than any other single factor, I think, has been the tailwind that’s propelled AI progress over the last 10 or 15 years. Warzel: And it’s what’s made them these companies just basically insatiable, right? In terms of how much they want to purchase. How much they want to use. Buchanan: That’s right. Yeah, it’s worth dwelling, for one second, just on the numbers here. Because they’re absolutely mind blowing. And they underscore one of the other important elements in the book and in our policy—which is that AI is the first revolutionary technology of the last hundred or so years that comes from the private sector. Think about nukes and space, and so much else, coming from the government. The government’s cutting the checks at a minimum, and has some capacity to steer where the technology goes. The modern paradigm of AI, this computing power–driven paradigm that we were just talking about, comes from the private sector. And it really is just eye-popping: the amount of investment the private sector is making in pursuit of the bitter lesson, or what’s sometimes called the scaling law. In 2026 alone, the estimates are that the hyperscalers, the big compute companies, will spend $700 billion on infrastructure and growing to a trillion or so dollars by 2027. Just taking the 2026 number, that’s akin to a Manhattan Project basically every two or three weeks. That’s more than America spent building the entire interstate-highway system, adjusting for inflation over 35 years. So it’s just so hard to overestimate the amount of computing power at play here in making these AI systems. Warzel: And it sets the stakes of this, I think, extremely well. Before we get into the nuts and bolts of this Nvidia story, I wanna step back; talk to a little bit about our technological relationship to China. You’ve said in the book, in the past, that AI will be the fulcrum on which the U.S.-China rivalry turns. So help me understand why that is. And also why it’s so bad that China gets access to these chips. Buchanan: We entered the White House in 2021 with the belief that AI would become very relevant, if not at the absolute center, of national-security affairs. Not just with China, but around the world. There’s a number of ways in which that importance could manifest over time, which we thought would take five or so years. Let’s take the one that’s the most concrete right now, and that’s cyber operations. It’s no secret that the United States and China engage every single day in cyber operations; cyber espionage against one another. That this is one of the key contours of competition between the two nations—that if you have an advantage in cyber operations, you have a substantial national-security advantage. I don’t think anyone can test that at this point. What was speculative in 2021—but that we believed would come to pass before too long—was that AI would change cyber operations. In 2026, it has. In 2026 alone, AI systems have discovered thousands, if not tens of thousands, of critical vulnerabilities in vital software all over the internet. The AI companies that have built this software, working in concert with the U.S. government, have turned these vulnerabilities over to vendors and to other network defenders, so that they can be patched and remediated. Essentially making the internet as a whole more secure. My belief, and I think this is pretty well supported, is that if China had access to such a technology and was finding these kinds of vulnerabilities in software, it would not be turning them over to be fixed and remediated. It would be using them for intelligence purposes. And that would put key parts of American critical infrastructure at risk. Just recently, this past week, as we’re recording this here, an AI company using an advanced AI system disclosed that they had found a vulnerability in Java, one of the absolute core languages that makes the modern economy go. A couple of weeks ago, the same company announced that they found a vulnerability in PHP, which is the back end for 70 percent of the websites on the internet. So we are talking about mega-vulnerabilities that AI systems are finding that have profound national-security implications in the wrong hand. And our view was certainly that it was better for the United States to get to that threshold first. Warzel: So you’ve also said that this race to unlock all these capabilities, including the cyber capabilities, may be “winner take all,” I think is how you described it. Help me understand why that’s a zero-sum game. Buchanan: I think we should be very precise here. So the dynamics are close to winner take all—which is to say, if you get to these critical thresholds first, then you can aggregate for yourself a lot of the power that comes from reaching those thresholds. We just gave the cyber example. I think there’s no doubt that the nation that got there first has a lot of power. What you choose to do with that power does not need to be zero sum. And in fact, I would argue throughout American history, a lot of the moments where American policymaking was at its best was when it had a fair amount of power and in some ways ceded that power to institutions, or built a stabilizing framework. So I don’t know that it’s zero sum in the geopolitical sense. Certainly, when I was in the government, we spent a lot of time trying to negotiate with China. And trying to say to China: Look, we’re taking competitive actions here, of course. But we think there’s interest, and that both of us have, that are shared. Let’s work on making this a positive-sum relationship. The Chinese largely blew us off. We can talk about it if you’d like. But this was certainly a key part of our overall AI strategy. Warzel: How would you describe the “they blew us off” part of that? Buchanan: So in October 2023, President Biden signed an executive order that included a line that when you translate from the legalese, essentially, said the United States will engage on AI safety—not just with its allies and its partners, but with its competitors. And that of course meant China. And President Biden personally took that line to President Xi [Jinping] three weeks later when the two leaders met in Woodside, California. And essentially he said: I’m serious about this. We have to work together on this and have a positive-sum relationship . The two leaders agreed to set up a dialogue of the AI experts in Geneva in May of ’24. It happened. I was there. It was maybe 10 or so U.S.-government officials, 10 or so Chinese-government officials. We took it incredibly seriously. We sent essentially everyone who was an AI leader in the U.S. government, went on this trip. The Chinese did not. And the Chinese subordinated it to their political apparatus, and spent the entire meeting essentially saying, like: We’re not sure why you’re talking about risks. We don’t see risks in AI. All this discussion of risks, even shared risks, is American imperialism. We pushed anyway. And we said, No, we really think there’s shared risks here. We really think there’s things we can do that are positive sum. Eventually, after six months of pushing on that point, we got the most common-sense thing, the thing that you should think would take six minutes. And that was an agreement between the two leaders, President Biden and President Xi, when they met for the last time, in November 2024—to not put AI in nuclear command and control. And I think we can all agree we don’t want AI firing nuclear weapons. So this should be the most simple thing in the world, but it took 13 months of pushing to get China to even get there. I’m hopeful China’s posture is different now. Certainly if we had had a second term, we would have—we were making plans to continue outreach to China on this point. But there wasn’t a lot of doubt in my mind that China was not, at the time, ready to have a serious conversation about shared interests and shared risks, and how we could all work together. Warzel: Do you have any sense of where you think China sits now on this? Given that, you know, the capabilities have skyrocketed? This is clearly a more of a top-of-mind geopolitical issue probably than it was, you know, during the Biden administration. Buchanan: I can point to some pieces of evidence that suggests China’s taking it more seriously. There’s some suggestion they’re thinking about cyber risks and talking to their companies about cyber risks. There’s some suggestion in some of the Chinese Communist Party publications that they’re warning about the dangers of AI and so forth. So I think there’s some evidence. And certainly, those are the threads I would be pulling if I were in the government. But also, China is essentially a nation run by one person. And I think it’s very hard, you know, even when you have access to U.S. intelligence to know exactly what Xi Jinping is thinking. I don’t have access to U.S. intelligence right now. So I wouldn’t wanna pretend to know what’s in his head when it comes to AI. And that, really, at the end of the day is the ultimate question when it comes to China. [ Break ] Warzel: So the Biden White House has a, you know, very specific policy about China having access to Nvidia’s chips. There’s a real focus on this amongst all the AI-policy folks, including yourself. Take me to [Jensen] Huang and Nvidia. What is Huang’s policy toward China when it comes to selling to them or around this period? Buchanan: He said the same thing in private that he said in public. Which is, we put this policy in place in 2022. We said to him, essentially: The supply of chips in the world is fixed, because it’s so hard to make them. There’s not gonna be that many more coming off the line. And we want those chips to not go to China. Because we’re worried they’re gonna modernize their military; they’re gonna repress their population with these surveillance tools and the like. Instead, we want those chips to go to the rest of the world, but especially companies in democratic nations. And Nvidia’s posture was that this would really hurt them; that this was bad for them economically. And that they needed the China market in order to compete. And sometimes, to give the sort of steel man of Jensen’s position, Jensen would often say things like—or Jensen and, I should say, his supporters, because there’s a whole group of folks who had this view—would say things like: Well, we need to keep China dependent on American chips. And we’ve got to sell them the chips, so they don’t make their own. We disagreed with the two prongs of that argument. The first prong we disagreed with was that this would be very bad for Nvidia. And essentially, our view was that the bitter lesson that we talked about before was so dominant, that the tailwinds of demand for American compute—I think you said the companies in the United States are insatiable when it comes to compute. That’s absolutely right. Jensen said that as well. And they would buy every single chip Nvidia made, and they would buy it for a significant profit. And that’s exactly what happened. Nvidia’s market capitalization in 2022, when we did the controls, was something like $350 billion. Just before the Jensen scandal a couple of weeks ago, it was $5 trillion. They’ve had a rough week here. But depending on how you do the math, they’re probably up 10 or 15 X on where they were when the compute control started, because of the tailwind that we foresaw about the scaling law and the bitter lesson and the demand for compute. So Nvidia has done great. And in fact, on the Nvidia earnings call just this week, when asked about a recent Trump action to close some of these loopholes and reassert export controls, they downplayed the impact of it, because they’re now acknowledging the demand is so big around the world. So we don’t think we were hurting Nvidia. We think Nvidia was going to do very well under our policy, and indeed they did. The second question is: Are we hurting the United States? Because, do the chip controls cause China to indigenize production in a way they wouldn’t otherwise have? And therefore we lose some leverage over China because they’re no longer dependent on American chips? I also think this was wrong, and we thought it was wrong at the time. The reason why is that China knew the importance of advanced chips. As far back as 2014, when America was off fighting ISIS, China recognized, up to the Xi Jinping level and the State Council of China, recognized how important chipmaking was. China at the time was spending more money importing chips than it was spending importing oil. And they couldn’t make any advanced chips at home. So Xi Jinping began an effort when you count the public and private capital upwards of $200 billion to build a chipmaking industry in China. So they had the pedal to the metal on indigenization before we ever took any action. The Trump administration, in their first term, made it a little bit harder. They cut China off the top end of equipment called EV machines—from the company I mentioned before, ASML. And then when we took the controls, we put the controls in place in 2022 on chips. We also put controls in place on chipmaking equipment, another generation of chipmaking equipment, which were imperfect, but what held China back. So the bottom line is even today, even despite the controls and despite China’s more than a decade-long effort to indigenize, chipmaking is so hard that China has failed. And don’t take my word for it: [Commerce Secretary Howard] Lutnick, one of the men at the center of this recent export-control story, testified in 2025 China can make just 200,000 chips. And together, 200,000 for the whole country is not nearly enough. It’s not even enough for a single data center. So those were Nvidia’s arguments, and what our responses were to them. Warzel: So in 2022, as you said, the U.S. implements these pretty sweeping export controls on semiconductors or on the chips. Can you briefly explain to me that policy in broad source for people who are not familiar with, you know, the export controls? Buchanan: Basically, our view was the risk of diversion was so high—that the chips could be sold to a civilian buyer, but would end up in PLA, the Chinese-military data centers, or end up in the domestic surveillance apparatus—that we had to control the sale of chips. Not just to the particular military buyers in China, but to the whole country. So the policy in 2022, and then some tightenings thereafter, was to say to companies like Nvidia: You may not sell your product; these advanced chips. You can sell lower-end chips, but you cannot sell these particular advanced chips into China, full stop . And that was a big step. Warzel: This is a dumb question, but what’s the penalty there? Buchanan: It’s a crime. The Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce have together pursued investigations to arrest and charge people who have violated U.S. export controls or smuggled chips into China, or things like that. Warzel: So the export controls, as I know it in the story, is ultimately one of the decisions that brings Huang and Nvidia—who are not, you know, huge political players leading up to this—more into the D.C. fold, right? It seems that a lot of like their advocacy, especially Huang’s, really ramps up in response to this. So I’m curious: Tell me how Nvidia started rolling up its sleeves and lobbying against those bans starting around 2022, when you guys put them in. Buchanan: We consulted with Nvidia as we were doing it, even before it happened. Because we were trying to understand the technology, and we were certainly not trying to surprise them out of the blue. So it’s not like they woke up one morning and said, Well, you know, the policy is in effect right now. So there were conversations all along. I think those conversations obviously intensified once the policy was in effect, and as we were making adjustments to it and so forth. But these were the reasonably standard conversations that the government has with companies. And you know, when I was the White House special adviser for AI, I talked to all the AI companies pretty regularly. I think it’s part of the job of the government, especially when the private sector is inventing the technology. It’s part of the job of the government to understand what they’re doing, and what its implications are. Warzel: But I’m curious. Like the tenor, the tone of it—as someone who had the opportunity to be in the room. I’ve seen some reports. There’s a report that I read recently from Semafor about Nvidia’s more recent lobbying efforts. Quoting an anonymous congressional staffer saying their MO has been largely gaslighting: creating an intense trust deficit between government, the Hill, and Nvidia. Like, were these conversations acrimonious? What’s the tenor of these conversations? Buchanan: I think they were strident, maybe even aggressive, but it didn’t bother me. I don’t—you know, I just felt like Jensen was doing his job, and talking his book. And those of us in the White House, and they were a group of us in the White House who had very strong conviction on this, felt like we were here to serve U.S. national security. And serve the public, and also serve American innovation. But we certainly felt like we had the technical depth to have detailed conversations with Nvidia, and we did. And you know, the policy ended where, I think, in general the policy should have ended. I would have probably been a little bit more aggressive, if you had asked me, in terms of some of the controls. But in general, I think the policy got to where it needed to be. Probably got there slower than it needed to get there. But in general, I’m happy with certainly our core strategic and technological thesis, which I think has been borne out at this point. Warzel: So now we’re at the current scandal. The affair with Alice Huang—no relation, and former executive at Megaspeed. Allegedly the Chinese intelligence asset. With the caveat that Megaspeed has denied all allegations of wrongdoing, can you explain a little bit about how this alleged chip smuggling works in practice? Buchanan: So I want to be clear here that I don’t have firsthand knowledge of Megaspeed. I’m only going off the news reports. I’ve left the U.S. government, obviously, in January 2025. But it does seem like Megaspeed is an exemplar of two categories of risk that worried us quite a bit when it comes to China’s access to chips. The first is that the chips themselves would be smuggled into China. So they would be purchased in a place like Malaysia or Singapore. There might be some facade of a buyer, potentially a company like Megaspeed in one of those places, that is taking the chips into their data center; is saying, Yes, we’re going to run them here. Everything is good. Don’t worry. And then they’re taking the chips out of the data center, and they’re shipping them into China. And they’re ending up in a Chinese-military data center or the data center of a company that works for the Chinese military, or something like that. And that obviously is a very significant concern for the United States, because that’s direct smuggling of the chips themselves. And we don’t know—once they go into China, we don’t know what the chips are going to be used for. The second category of concern is what’s called remote access. The chips still go to a kind of shady company in Malaysia or Singapore, or a place like that. They go into a data center, but they stay there. The difference is China—Chinese military, Chinese companies—just access that data center remotely over the internet. So the chips stay there, but China can train their next-frontier AI system on this data center, remote. So it’s a different way of circumvent export controls. And we made a decision in one of the export-control updates to try to block that. To say: As a condition of taking these chips, you have to pledge that you will not use them to enable Chinese AI training. President Trump, when he came into office, declined to enforce that rule. So there’s at least a legal gray space—of maybe it was permitted, or the administration wasn’t enforcing it. But those are the two big categories of concern: the actual physical smuggling of the chip, and then the remote access. It’s worth saying Nvidia spent a great deal of time in 2025 and 2026, including Jensen personally, saying chip smuggling is not an issue. And I think it’s obviously incorrect. Not just because of the Megaspeed case, but also because of other cases in which the Department of Justice has brought really well-documented indictments and criminal charges against people for smuggling chips in the way that I described. Warzel: In terms of that remote access to those data centers that are outside of China, for training purposes, it’s known that China has distilled—or sort of reverse-engineered, you know—U.S. models in order to kind of keep up in the race here. Is that where that is happening in your mind? Like, inside those places? Or is that happening more locally? Or is it a mix of the two? Buchanan: Assume it’s a mix. So let’s just be very precise about what’s happening. Distillation is a process in which you can essentially—you know, if folks here are Formula 1 fans, you can draft behind the car in front of you. And you can get the outputs of a leading AI system and come up with the facsimile of that system, imperfectly. You’ll lag capabilities, but it’s cheaper. That is a general concern. And one of the ways in which China has been trying to compensate for the lack of computing power. Essentially, is copying the Americans’ homework. That process of distillation still requires some computing power. And I would imagine China is using whatever computing power it has available to do the process of distillation, whether that’s chips overseas or chips in China. Companies have gotten much better at stopping distillation. So Anthropic, a company that I advise, but I don’t speak for, reported that they came up with methods in the summer of 2026 to stop distillation. I think it was like up to like 99 percent. And I think OpenAI is making some moves in that direction as well. So my suspicion, hard to know for sure, is that we will look at this kind of adversarial distillation as an artifact of a period from 2025 to 2026 where China really struggled with access to computing power, in part due to the export controls, and was using distillation as a way to try to keep up with the frontier. But I don’t think that will be sustainable for them in the long run. And then they’ll be back to the same box of not having enough computing power. [ Break ] Warzel: Given what we’ve learned about Megaspeed, and what you’ve said about the Department of Justice also bringing cases about people trying to, you know, navigate around these export controls—what is your sense of just how much Nvidia helped China get access to these chips? Like, how bad is this going to get for Jensen, for Nvidia, in terms of where this can go? Buchanan: It’s a great question. Again, I don’t have firsthand knowledge of the facts here, and I don’t want to pretend. It does seem like the amount of chips going through these channels was really significant, potentially even more than the number of chips China could make as a whole country itself. I think The Wall Street Journal reported something like $12 billion of chips. I’ve seen other reportings saying it was $4 billion to $5 billion of chips. Megaspeed is just one company. There were other companies that were potentially doing this. What Nvidia knew, what Jensen knew—that is all for congressional and maybe criminal investigators to find out. I don’t pretend to know. But certainly, as a national-security matter, I do think that the flow of chips to China in this way—smuggling and through remote data centers—is one of the biggest national-security weaknesses the United States has. And what you’ve seen really is a pretty clear bipartisan consensus to change the policy. And there’s bipartisan bills in the Congress—introduced by, you know, MAGA senators like Tom Cotton and Jim Banks, and people like that—that would cut China off chips and chipmaking equipment as a matter of law. So the president couldn’t change it, even if he wanted to. And then, even the Trump administration, this past Monday, changed their policy and cut off remote access to data centers and required licenses for shipments to Southeast Asia to try to cut off the smuggling. They’re not quite done; there’s still a couple loopholes in their rule. But that was a very significant action for an administration that really, you know, from the middle of 2025 to today, was only taking export controls away and not enforcing them, rather than putting them into practice. Warzel: So there are calls from Silicon Valley right—from the shareholders, from the, you know, VC types, the other tech founders of some esteem. They want Jensen Huang to come back. He’s a visionary; he’s integral to the AI economy . Help me understand the rationale here, because China is enemy No. 1 in terms of the race to superintelligence. But also, it just seems like they’re abandoning the China fears all of a sudden, or excusing this dalliance. This potential dalliance. Buchanan: I think a lot of the folks who are making those calls—which, to be clear, the Nvidia board pretty clearly rejected on their earnings call this week. A lot of that constellation of people has been pretty dismissive of the China concern. So they’re often the ones supporting selling chips to China. So at least they’re consistent on that front, in that they’re just not worried about this. I think there’s probably a key difference between my view and their view. Which is: I think AI really is going to matter for national security. And at least their revealed preference is they don’t think that, because they’re willing to let China in the game. But as a national-security matter, I certainly am very concerned and think these activities should be investigated. Warzel: What is so hard for me to understand with that is that the national-security imperative is part of the imperative of the companies, that are saying: We can’t afford to truly pace the frontier— or “stop” or “pause” or whatever —because it’s imperative that we beat China to this. I mean, I do feel like they’re speaking out of both corners of their mouth here. Buchanan: I do think, yeah. So if what you’re saying is sometimes the same people who are saying We can’t regulate AI are also saying Let’s sell chips to China. I mean: We can’t regulate AI, because we have to beat China are also saying Let’s sell chips to China . I agree. That is totally incoherent. It doesn’t make any sense to me. President Trump himself—in, you know, militaristic terms that I would not use, given our discussion before about how we hope to have a positive-sum outcome here—President Trump is very fond of saying: Whoever wins AI, wins . You would think if that is your policy, you would not want to sell chips to China. I don’t get it. I think it’s incoherent for the reason you describe. To be clear about what I do believe, my view is: American companies in fact do have to slow down. And I support pacing the frontier. We haven’t talked about it, but you know, part two of the book is all about how we regulated the AI companies, and what more we need to do on the regulation side. That was sort of huge part of our policy. And my view is that, in fact, the way in which we can create the space for regulation—as far back as 2021, we believed—was to slow China down. And China’s absolute dependence on American computing power was a way for us to slow China down, to build a lead for the United States. And then to, if you’d like, spend that lead on safety, to when the technology got to a critical moment. Which is what we’re in right now. To regulate the companies pretty aggressively, if I had my way. To make sure this technology is safe before it’s rolled out. Without this argument of: Well, we’re in an arms race with China; we must forge ahead . Which I thought was just very destructive. Warzel: So where does this all leave us right now, as we’re sitting in the story here? We’re talking Wednesday, November 18th. Obviously, things are changing by the minute. Buchanan: Always good to timestamp these conversations, ’cause it’s been changing every 24 hours. Warzel: Genuinely, it is. How much hot water is Jensen in? How dangerous and serious is this for Nvidia, as Huang goes to testify before Congress in December? Like, what are the stakes for both Huang and Nvidia going forward? Buchanan: I think they’re very high. Congress, in a bipartisan way, said it’s gonna do an investigation here. I don’t know what’s gonna turn up, but certainly they’ve got a lot of threads to pull. Whether or not there’s a criminal investigation, I have no idea. But I do suspect there will be a lot of government investigations into what happened here, and there should be. I guess in the medium term, Nvidia’s chips are still gonna be really good, and there’s still gonna be big demand for them. So as long as Nvidia can keep making great products, I think they will continue to sell those products. I guess it’s an open question of: Can they make great products without Jensen? We’ll see. They’ve got 31,000 research engineers, or something like that. So there’s a lot of smart people there, and they’ve got a lot of great technology. So we’ll see what happens to them technologically. But yeah; in the context of the investigations, certainly I would describe this as a serious moment. Warzel: What should senators be asking? Or what should anyone in Congress be asking Huang when he’s up there, you know, in front of Congress? Buchanan: It’s the most important, age-old question in any kind of D.C. investigation, which is: What did you know, and when did you know it? And they should be asking Jensen that, and they should be asking the commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, that. Who knew what about where these chips were going. Who was getting them. How active was Nvidia’s role in enabling smuggling? How active was Jensen’s role? Again, I don’t have firsthand knowledge of the answers. But those were all the questions I’d be asking. Warzel: And I think lastly here, what has this done for the AI ecosystem right now? Like, is it in a worse place than it was? Or let’s just say, the American AI ecosystem? Is it in a worse place than it was two weeks ago, before all of this stuff really trickled out into the press? Or it was about the same? Buchanan: I think it probably creates some turbulence in the waters, but my suspicion is we’ll look back at this in six or 12 months, and the big story of AI will be largely unchanged by this. And the big story of AI, you know—as we spent a lot of detail on the book—is: You have really powerful chips being used by really capable algorithms, at larger and larger scales. Yielding extraordinarily capable systems, with profound national-security implications and profound implications for everyday life and democratic values. That story. To be clear, I’m not a cheerleader for that story. You know, you don’t write a book called The Bitter Struggle if you’re a cheerleader. But I think that story is largely undiminished by these events here. Warzel: What about China? Where are they better off? Are they worse off than they were? Buchanan: They’re worse off. They’re absolutely worse off. Because there was a bipartisan consensus that was forming on denying China access to computing power. But they had big allies that were saying, You know, let’s sell China the chips . And those allies were having some success. Chief amongst some, Jensen. David Sacks, Trump’s—my successor, as you know—AI adviser to the president, was advocating for this, at least based on the reporting. President Trump had advocated for in some context. And now the bipartisan consensus has, at least so far, started to harden against them. That is bad for China’s access to compute, and ultimately that is bad for China. Warzel: Ben Buchanan: Thank you for coming and helping to demystify this; talking about it in these very plain terms. I wanna have you back on, to talk about the regulation part of this, later. But this has been very helpful. Buchanan: It is great to talk about this subject, and it’s great to have interest in this subject of the chips and chip controls. Because this is a wonky subject for sure—that now has gotten this gloss of a sex scandal and a spy story. But I don’t think it’s an exaggeration to say this is one of the most important subjects in the world for U.S. national policy. Warzel: And we’ll keep following it. Thank you very much, Ben, for coming on. Buchanan: Thanks for having me. [ Music ] Warzel: If you liked what you saw here, new episodes of Galaxy Brain drop every Friday. You can subscribe on The Atlantic ’s YouTube channel, or on Apple or Spotify, or wherever it is that you get your podcasts. And if you want to support this work, and the work of my fellow colleagues, you can subscribe to the publication at TheAtlantic.com/Listener. That’s TheAtlantic.com/Listener. Thanks so much, and I’ll see you on the internet. This episode of Galaxy Brain was produced by Hadley Robinson, with story editing by Dave Shaw; the video was edited by Alisa Selman; and the audio was engineered by Rob Smierciak. Claudine Ebeid is the executive producer of Atlantic podcasts, and Andrea Valdez is our managing editor.Learn more about your ad choices. Visit podcastchoices.com/adchoices

﻿ 以下是上周西太平洋主要舰船活动和演习的摘要。 2026 年 11 月 11 日，新加坡，隶属第 13 海军陆战队远征部队海军陆战队中型倾转旋翼机中队 (VMM) 364（增援）的一名美国海军陆战队员正在准备一架 MV-22B 鱼鹰，以便在黄蜂级两栖攻击舰马金岛号 (LHD-8) 上起飞。美国海军陆战队照片周五，两栖攻击舰马金岛号根据当地船舶观察员和 AIS 数据，两栖船坞运输舰 LHD-8（LHD-8）和两栖船坞运输舰 USS John P. Murtha（LPD-26）已驶入新加坡三巴旺。马金岛和约翰·P·穆萨号与两栖运输船坞舰安克雷奇号 (LPD-23) 和已上船的第 13 海军陆战队远征部队组成了马金岛两栖待命大队。安克雷奇仍停靠在日本横须贺司令舰队活动中心。 2026 年 11 月 14 日，美国海军水手长三等大副马修·普里米蒂沃（左）和水手长二等大副杰伦·斯罗克莫顿在新加坡海上抛锚期间将千斤顶杆固定在独立型濒海战斗舰塔尔萨号（LCS-16）上。美国海军照片濒海战斗舰塔尔萨号（LCS-16）驶入新加坡周六出发，周一出发。塔尔萨隶属于第七驱逐舰中队（DESRON），该中队部署在东南亚前沿，是东南亚行动区指定舰艇的主要战术和作战指挥官。
在菲律宾马尼拉，澳大利亚总理安东尼·艾博内塞于 2026 年 11 月 15 日在菲律宾马尼拉参观澳大利亚皇家海军舰队加油船 HMAS Stalwart (A304)。澳大利亚国防军照片 澳大利亚皇家海军舰队加油船 HMAS Stalwart (A304) 对马尼拉进行港口访问。周日，正在出席东南亚国家联盟（ASEAN）峰会的澳大利亚总理安东尼·阿尔巴内斯（Anthony Albanese）访问了这艘船，会见了船员和在菲律宾的澳大利亚国防军人员。 Stalwart 正在进行区域部署。 2026 年 11 月 16 日，南海，美国海军燃气轮机系统技术员（机械）海员谢恩·文森特（来自肯塔基州）在南海将军区斑马训练期间，对阿利·伯克级导弹驱逐舰拉尔夫·约翰逊号 (DDG-114) 上的通道中的斑马配件进行注释。美国海军照片 驱逐舰拉尔夫·约翰逊号（DDG-114）于周日穿越吕宋海峡，截至周一正在南海作业。拉尔夫·约翰逊（Ralph Johnson）前沿部署并分配到日本基地的DESRON 15。在越南海防，法国海军护卫舰FS Vendémiaire（F734）周一与越南海岸警卫队8004号近海巡逻船进行了联合搜救演习。此次演习是在法国护卫舰于11月12日开始访问海防后离开海防之后进行的。 Vendémiaire 总部位于新喀里多尼亚努美阿。

一年中的大部分时间里，莱特纳平原都没有什么可以为当地人或游客提供的东西。这是布拉格斯巴达足球场对面的一大片毫无特色的土地。表面交替出现灰尘和泥土；有一个巴士停车场，有时还有马戏团。但莱特纳偶尔会举办一些可以让捷克政坛发生倾斜的活动。有时有一点。有时很多。 1989 年 11 月 25 日星期六，大约 75 万人聚集在一起，要求结束捷克斯洛伐克的共产主义政权。第二天，许多人返回，并于 11 月 29 日星期三，议会废除了共产党在社会中的领导地位。这次不会再发生类似的事情，但 11 月 15 日星期日，莱特纳岛上大约有 40 万人参加了自天鹅绒革命以来布拉格最大规模的示威活动。从媒体平台俯瞰旗帜和面孔的海洋时，它看起来很大。数万人聚集在那里抗议政府计划取消每月 10 美元的许可费，该许可费为该国两家公共广播公司捷克电视台和捷克广播电台提供资金。这似乎不是一个令人愤慨的提议，但对许多捷克人来说，这加深了他们对亿万富翁总理安德烈·巴比什及其民粹主义联盟的不信任。这位总理多年来一直在法庭上与欧盟补贴欺诈指控作斗争，他不喜欢公共广播。

For much of the year, Letná Plain has nothing to offer either locals or tourists.  It’s a large, featureless patch of land opposite the Sparta Prague football stadium. The surface alternates between dust and mud; there’s a car park for buses, and sometimes a circus. But every so often, Letná hosts an event that can tilt the world of Czech politics on its axis. Sometimes a little. Sometimes a lot.  On Saturday, November 25, 1989, around 750,000 people gathered to demand the end of Czechoslovakia’s communist regime. The following day, many returned, and on Wednesday, November 29, parliament abolished the Communist Party’s leading role in society. Nothing like that is going to happen this time around, but on Sunday, November 15, there were perhaps 400,000 people on Letná for the largest demonstration in Prague since the Velvet Revolution. It looked huge when viewed from a media platform overlooking an ocean of flags and faces.   The people who had gathered in the tens of thousands were there to protest against government plans to scrap the $10 monthly license fee which funds the nation’s two public broadcasters, Czech TV and Czech Radio. This may not seem an outrageous proposal, but to many Czechs it deepens their distrust of their billionaire Prime Minister Andrej Babiš and his populist coalition.   The premier, who has spent years in court fighting EU subsidy fraud allegations , is no fan of public broadcasting.  Get the Latest Sign up to receive regular emails and stay informed about CEPA's work. In 2017, Babiš, who was then finance minister, described Czech TV’s investigative reporters as “a corrupt rabble making reports to order.” In 2024, he said public broadcasters were part of the then governing coalition’s “media division.”  But it is his coalition ally, the far-right SPD party, that has spearheaded the campaign to scrap the license fees and replace them with direct state funding. The fear is that state funds will come with strings pulled by politicians. Tokyo-born businessman Tomio Okamura, the SPD chairman and now parliament’s speaker, has said he would vote for a bill to abolish the broadcasters altogether if someone submitted one.  The third coalition partner is the MAGA-friendly Motorists for Themselves party, which was against scrapping the fees but is now in favor. One Motorist MP said public broadcasting had been turned into a totem by one half of Czech society, which was giving the other half the finger.  What is clear is that the government has not covered itself in glory. After months of vague and occasionally rancorous debate, and just days after all three coalition parties did poorly in Senate and local elections, the first reading of the bill was rushed through parliament in the middle of the night, with a vote scheduled for 4:36 am on Saturday, October 24. The bill envisages a cut in funding of around 15%, reversing an increase introduced by the previous government. Babiš is also floating alternative funding mechanisms, including voluntary contributions, and insists the government will not interfere in editorial decisions.  But there is a glaring contradiction. His government’s own impact assessment identifies the license fee as the funding mechanism that carries the smallest risk to the broadcasters’ independence. Direct state funding, it says, carries the greatest risk.  There has been much talk of “the Nordic model,” without acknowledging that there is no single Nordic model. Finland and Sweden, for example, have dedicated levies collected through the tax system, but Babiš has ruled out a new tax.  Observers are more worried about “the Slovak model.” There, the license fee was abolished in 2023 with a solemn promise to ringfence funding for Slovak Radio and TV and preserve its independence.  The following year, the broadcaster was dissolved by Robert Fico’s populist nationalist government and replaced. Critics say its successor is now toeing the government line. Babiš said he would not be deterred by mass demonstrations, though there was a tiny wobble from Culture Minister Oto Klempíř, who said after talks with Michael McGrath, the European Commissioner for Democracy and Justice, that he wanted to delay further debate on the bill until parliament had begun discussing legislation to implement the European Media Freedom Act.  The 72-year-old prime minister is in a tough spot. He seems tired and barely invested in the issue while his far-right coalition partner insists the fee has to go. Babiš is known to dislike big demonstrations, and the opposition senses an opportunity.  Following Klempíř’s suggestion to kick the issue into the long grass would be a logical course of action for the prime minister, but it may not be one that’s open to him.  Rob Cameron is a Prague-based journalist and broadcaster, and author of https://www.basedinbohemia.com/ where he writes about Central Europe through reporting, analysis and long-form storytelling. He is a regular contributor to a number of international broadcasters, including Deutsche Welle, RTÉ and Monocle Radio. zh_title: 铜价陷入熊市，抹去2026年涨幅，为今年最糟糕的一周
summary: 铜价周五再次暴跌，在创下历史新高仅十周后，铜价就进入熊市，因为对人工智能热潮的押注解除、强势美元和美国关税前景的黯淡继续掩盖了中国严重短缺的证据。纽约最活跃合约 Comex 12 月交割铜价一度下跌 3.4%，至每磅 5.4405 美元（每吨 11,994 美元），为 3 月底以来的最低水平，午盘左右回升至 5.4995 美元，跌幅 2.4%。这比 9 月 9 日达成的创纪录的 6.8885 美元结算价低 20.2%。收盘价低于 5 美元。
content:
铜价周五再次暴跌，在创下历史新高仅十周后，铜价就进入熊市，因为对人工智能热潮的押注解除、强势美元和美国关税前景的黯淡继续掩盖了中国严重短缺的证据。纽约最活跃合约 Comex 12 月交割铜价一度下跌 3.4%，至每磅 5.4405 美元（每吨 11,994 美元），为 3 月底以来的最低水平，午盘左右回升至 5.4995 美元，跌幅 2.4%。这比 9 月 9 日创下的 6.8885 美元的创纪录结算价低 20.2%。收盘价低于 5.51 美元将符合熊市的常见定义，即较最近的峰值下跌 20% 或更多。该合约已连续七个交易日下跌，自上周五以来已下跌超过 9%，为 2026 年迄今为止最大单周跌幅。9 月份迄今为止的涨幅为 22%，目前已下跌 2%，而铜价到 11 月底预计将下跌约 15%。据路透社报道，伦敦金属交易所三个月期铜在官方交易中下跌 2.3%，至每吨 12,235 美元，此前触及 12,020 美元，为 3 月 24 日以来的最低水平。该基准指数本周下跌约 9%，这是自 2025 年 4 月初美国总统唐纳德·特朗普公布全球关税以来的最大单周跌幅。伦敦铜价比 9 月 10 日峰值 14,875 美元低 18%，并且必须跌破 11,900 美元才能与纽约市一样进入熊市。
据彭博社报道，在上海，期货创下了 15 年来最糟糕的一周。下一站，3 月份的低点，跌破 5.63 美元（2025 年铜价结束时的价格），消除了盛宝银行 (Saxo Bank) 的 Ole Hansen 在周三暴跌期间标记的两个图表支撑中的第一个。第二个价格为 5.32 美元，略低于 2026 年的最低收盘价：3 月 20 日的 5.34 美元，当时伊朗战争期间油价飙升和交易所库存膨胀导致金属跌至三个月低点。目前铜价比该水平高出不到 3%。 Capital.com 高级金融市场分析师凯尔·罗达 (Kyle Rodda) 向路透社表示，越来越多的证据表明，人工智能投资热潮正在减弱，美联储将不得不更加积极地控制通胀，并补充说，美元走强也给黄金带来压力。该通讯社称，周五 AI 股价继续下跌，Anthropic 上市后股价较周四收盘价下跌约 9%。 Benchmark Mineral Intelligence 的铜分析师 Albert Mackenzie 告诉彭博社：“只要人工智能一直在推动价格上涨，我们就一直在说，这可能有点过分了。”中国需求疲软、美国关税和美元前景黯淡也在发挥作用，本周的损失与大流行初期和特朗普宣布解放日之后的暴跌相差不远。伦敦铜正面临 2022 年以来最大幅度的月度跌幅。
金属流向中国 期货抛售仍在继续，同时中国对实物金属的争夺仍在继续。 据路透社报道，周五，进口铜到中国所支付的洋山溢价从周四创纪录的每吨 500 美元下滑至 495 美元。周三价格为 360 美元，9 月份还不到 100 美元。上海期货交易所库存本周增加 3,204 吨至 30,846 吨，仍低于中国一天的消费量。这种紧张可能是导致期货下跌的部分原因。这些水平的溢价使得将金属运出美国变得有利可图，过去一年美国库存激增

【原文 English Original】
Copper slumped again on Friday, tipping the metal into a bear market just ten weeks after it set an all-time high, as the unwinding of bets on the artificial intelligence boom, a strong dollar and fading US tariff prospects continued to swamp evidence of acute shortage in China. Comex copper for December delivery, the most active contract in New York, dropped as much as 3.4% to $5.4405 a pound ($11,994 a tonne), the lowest since the end of March, before recovering to $5.4995 around midday, down 2.4%. That is 20.2% below the record settlement of $6.8885 reached on September 9. A close under $5.51 would meet the common definition of a bear market, a fall of 20% or more from the most recent peak. The contract has fallen for seven sessions in a row and is down more than 9% since last Friday, by far its steepest weekly loss of 2026. A year-to-date gain that stood at 22% in September has turned into a loss of 2%, and copper is on course to end November about 15% lower. On the London Metal Exchange, three-month copper fell 2.3% to $12,235 a tonne in official trading after touching $12,020, the lowest since March 24, Reuters reports. The benchmark is down about 9% on the week, its biggest weekly fall since early April 2025, when US President Donald Trump unveiled his global tariffs. London copper is 18% below its September 10 peak of $14,875 and would have to drop under $11,900 to join New York in a bear market. In Shanghai, futures racked up their worst week in 15 years, according to Bloomberg. Next stop, the March low The break below $5.63, where copper ended 2025, removes the first of two chart supports that Saxo Bank’s Ole Hansen flagged during Wednesday’s rout . The second is $5.32, which sits just beneath the lowest close of 2026: $5.34 on March 20, when surging oil prices during the Iran war and swelling exchange inventories sent the metal to a three-month trough. Copper is now less than 3% above that level. Evidence is mounting that the AI investment boom is waning and that the Federal Reserve will have to get more aggressive to control inflation, Kyle Rodda, senior financial market analyst at Capital.com, told Reuters, adding that a strengthening dollar is also weighing on the metal. AI shares continued to sag on Friday, with Anthropic trading about 9% below Thursday’s close after its market debut, the news agency said. “We have been saying for as long as AI has been driving the price that this might be a bit over-egged,” Albert Mackenzie, copper analyst at Benchmark Mineral Intelligence, told Bloomberg. Weak Chinese demand, the dimming prospect of US tariffs and the dollar are also at work, and the week’s losses are not far off the slumps seen in the early stages of the pandemic and after Trump’s Liberation Day announcement. London copper is heading for its steepest monthly decline since 2022 . Metal heads to China The selloff in futures is still running alongside a scramble for physical metal in China. The Yangshan premium paid to import copper into the country slipped to $495 a tonne on Friday from Thursday’s record $500, Reuters reports. It was $360 on Wednesday and less than $100 in September. Shanghai Futures Exchange stocks rose by 3,204 tonnes this week to 30,846 tonnes, which is still less than a day’s worth of Chinese consumption. That tightness may be part of what is pushing futures down. Premiums at these levels have made it profitable to move metal out of the United States, where stockpiles ballooned over the past year on tariff bets, and traders have begun shipping copper from the US to China , with tens of thousands of tonnes due to arrive in January. Codelco is meanwhile offering Chinese buyers 2027 cathode at $250 to $280 a tonne , less than it charged this year. The flow looks set to continue. China’s refined copper imports are poised to climb in 2027 after a rare drop this year, according to a Reuters poll of 15 analysts and traders, because shortages of concentrate and scrap are holding back domestic smelter output while demand keeps growing. Imports fell 16% to 2.37 million tonnes in the first ten months of 2026, the lowest for the period since at least 2015. “The gravitational pull of refined copper is now towards China,” said Nicholas Snowdon, head of metals and mining research at Mercuria, although Argus expects a moderate recovery rather than a surge. In London the squeeze has eased: cash copper was at only a slight premium to the three-month contract on Friday after flipping into a discount earlier in the week. $127 billion in a week Copper stocks were sold again in New York. Eleven of the largest copper-exposed miners have lost a combined $127 billion, or 15% of their market value, since last Friday, and $208 billion, or 23%, over the past month. Their combined worth has dropped to $696 billion from $769 billion on Wednesday morning. Freeport-McMoRan fell another 5.4%, taking its loss for the week to 22% and cutting its market value to $67 billion, from close to $100 billion a month ago. Southern Copper gave up 4.3% to $116 billion and has shed 32% in a month, a slide that has pushed the stock into the red for 2026 after it was up 41% in mid-October. BHP was little changed at $177 billion but is down 14% on the week, and Rio Tinto eased 1.3% to $127 billion. Glencore, at $71 billion, has lost a fifth of its value in a month. Teck Resources dropped 3.6% to $24 billion, Antofagasta 4.8% and First Quantum Minerals 3.7%, and Lundin Mining’s 2.3% decline left it 19% lower since last Friday. Only BHP, Glencore, Teck and Anglo American are still showing gains for the year, and Anglo’s is down to 1%. Ivanhoe Mines has lost 60% in 2026. (With files from Reuters and Bloomberg)

title: Ground View Pakistan: The smelter before the mine
zh_title: 巴基斯坦地面景观：矿井前的冶炼厂
summary: 在全球精炼能力已经超过现有精矿供应的情况下，巴基斯坦建立国内铜加工业的雄心可能会让冶炼厂领先于矿山。总理谢巴兹·谢里夫在伊斯兰堡举行的巴基斯坦矿产投资论坛 (PMIF) 上强调了这一雄心，承诺结束未加工矿物的出口，并呼吁西南部的雷科迪克项目和其他项目支持炼油厂、冶炼厂以及生产电缆和导体的工厂。 “在巴基斯坦开采，在巴基斯坦加工，在巴基斯坦制造，然后出口到世界其他地区
content:
在全球精炼能力已经超过现有精矿供应的情况下，巴基斯坦建立国内铜加工业的雄心可能会让冶炼厂领先于矿山。总理谢巴兹·谢里夫在伊斯兰堡举行的巴基斯坦矿产投资论坛 (PMIF) 上强调了这一雄心，承诺结束未加工矿物的出口，并呼吁西南部的雷科迪克项目和其他项目支持炼油厂、冶炼厂以及生产电缆和导体的工厂。谢里夫说：“在巴基斯坦开采，在巴基斯坦加工，在巴基斯坦制造，然后出口到世界其他地区。”这一举措反映出巴基斯坦希望从矿产财富中获取更多就业机会、技能和出口收入。但由于只有山达克 (Saindak) 一家铜矿生产厂，其旗舰 Reko Diq 项目仍在等待商业生产，该国面临着更紧迫的挑战：在投入数十亿美元建设加工基础设施之前建立可靠的矿山产出。巴基斯坦联邦规划、发展和特别倡议部长阿赫桑·伊克巴尔表示，政府现在要求投资者提交完整的价值链提案，而不是仅仅关注开采和原材料出口的计划。这一要求给探险家带来了特殊的挑战。铜冶炼厂是围绕特定精矿设计的，包括其品位、杂质和预期产量。
如果没有明确的矿产资源和可靠的生产，开发商就无法做出贷款人要求的原料承诺。Milbank 律师事务所能源和基础设施合伙人穆尼布·侯赛因 (Munib Hussain) 表示，合同原料是此类项目融资的主要要求之一。区别很重要。 2025 年 4 月，我认为仅靠采矿并不能实现关键的矿产独立性，因此应优先考虑对加工的投资。这一论点涉及美国，美国现有的矿藏和数十年的生产为下游投资奠定了基础。巴基斯坦正处于早期阶段，全球铜市场呈现出不同的经济现实。冶炼经济 随着中国的新设施与印度、中亚和非洲不断扩大的业务展开竞争，铜冶炼厂正面临产能过剩的困境。处理和精炼费用方面的压力显而易见，矿工向冶炼厂支付费用，将精矿转化为精炼金属。安托法加斯塔和中国冶炼厂同意 2026 年基准为每吨 0 美元和每磅 0 美分，低于 2025 年每吨 21.25 美元和前一年的 80 美元。现货费用已降至零以下，标准普尔全球普氏能源资讯 (S&P Global Platts) 1 月份的评估值为每吨负 47.40 美元。这些负费用意味着加工商实际上正在向矿工支付费用以确保精矿。
Wood Mackenzie 副总裁兼金属和采矿咨询主管帕特里克·巴恩斯 (Patrick Barnes) 在论坛上表示：“现在是建设冶炼厂的非常艰难的时期。”印度说明了其中的商业风险。阿达尼 (Adani) 价值 12 亿美元的卡奇铜冶炼厂每年需要约 160 万吨精矿才能满负荷运营。彭博社报道的进口记录显示，该公司在 2024 年 2 月至 2026 年 2 月期间获得了所需原料的四分之一以上。有关高杂质精矿相关运营不稳定的报道加剧了人们的担忧，尽管阿达尼对这些说法提出了异议。在其他地方，嘉能可关闭了位于菲尔州的帕萨尔冶炼厂

【原文 English Original】
Pakistan’s ambition to build a domestic copper processing industry risks putting smelters ahead of mines at a time when global refining capacity already exceeds available concentrate supplies.  Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif reinforced that ambition at the Pakistan Minerals Investment Forum (PMIF) in Islamabad, pledging to end exports of unprocessed minerals and calling for Reko Diq and other projects in the southwest to support refineries, smelters and factories producing cables and conductors.  “Mine in Pakistan, process in Pakistan, manufacture in Pakistan and then export to the rest of the world,” Sharif said.  The push reflects a desire to capture more jobs, skills and export revenue from Pakistan’s mineral wealth. But with only one producing copper operation, at Saindak, and its flagship Reko Diq project still awaiting commercial production, the country faces a more immediate challenge: establishing reliable mine output before committing billions to processing infrastructure.  Ahsan Iqbal, Pakistan’s federal minister of planning, development and special initiatives, said the government now asks investors to submit complete value-chain proposals rather than plans focused solely on extraction and raw-material exports.  That requirement creates a particular challenge for explorers. Copper smelters are designed around specific concentrates, including their grades, impurities and expected volumes. Without defined mineral resources and dependable production, developers cannot establish the feedstock commitments lenders require.  Munib Hussain, an energy and infrastructure partner at law firm Milbank, said contracted feedstock ranks among the principal requirements for financing such projects.  The distinction is important. In April 2025, I argued that mining alone would not deliver critical minerals independence and that investment in processing should take priority.  That argument concerned the United States, where established mineral deposits and decades of production provided a foundation for downstream investment. Pakistan is at an earlier stage, and the global copper market presents a different economic reality.  Smelting economics  Copper smelters are struggling with excess capacity as new facilities in China compete with expanding operations in India, Central Asia and Africa.  The pressure is evident in treatment and refining charges, which miners pay smelters to convert concentrate into refined metal.  Antofagasta and Chinese smelters agreed to a 2026 benchmark of $0 per tonne and zero cents per pound, down from $21.25 per tonne in 2025 and $80 the previous year. Spot charges have fallen below zero, with S&P Global Platts assessing them at minus $47.40 per tonne in January.  Those negative charges mean processors are effectively paying miners to secure concentrate.  “It’s a very tough time to build a smelter,” Patrick Barnes, vice-president and head of metals and mining consulting at Wood Mackenzie, said at the forum.  India illustrates the commercial risks. Adani’s $1.2-billion Kutch Copper smelter requires approximately 1.6 million tonnes of concentrate annually to operate at full capacity. Import records reported by Bloomberg indicate it secured just over a quarter of its required feedstock between February 2024 and February 2026.  Reports of operating instability linked to high-impurity concentrate have added to concerns, although Adani has disputed those accounts.  Elsewhere, Glencore has closed its Pasar smelter in the Philippines, while Australia has intervened to support the Mount Isa smelter in Queensland.  Even countries that have developed mines before building processing facilities remain exposed to supply disruptions.  Indonesia delayed its copper concentrate export restrictions until production at Grasberg, one of the world’s largest copper mines, could adequately supply domestic smelters. Freeport also had to demonstrate that sufficient concentrate had been reserved for its Manyar facility.  But a September 2025 mud rush at Grasberg forced Freeport to declare force majeure, leaving Indonesian processors short of material.  For Pakistan, these examples strengthen the commercial case for Reko Diq’s existing development plan.  The project is designed to export copper concentrate by rail to Port Qasim for shipment through the Pakistan International Bulk Terminal. Although that approach falls short of the government’s downstream ambitions, it positions Pakistan to benefit from the current shortage of concentrate rather than compete in an oversupplied smelting market.  Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb said Reko Diq’s first year of commercial production had been expected to generate $2.8 billion in exports, equivalent to roughly 10% of Pakistan’s current goods exports.  For an economy repeatedly constrained by balance-of-payments crises, that potential foreign exchange revenue is significant.  The opportunity also extends to Western supply chains. American and allied processors need dependable mineral supplies, making Pakistan’s emerging mining industry potentially more valuable as a concentrate exporter than as another entrant into copper smelting.  Domestic processing could still make economic sense for smaller, specialized operations targeting minerals with genuine refining bottlenecks and committed buyers. Antimony is one example, with at least one Pakistani processor pursuing refining capacity linked to prospective US offtake.  Exploration incentives  Pakistan’s taxation policies present another obstacle to establishing the mining industry needed to support future processing.  Waleed Ahmed Vohra, founder and chief executive of Pakistani explorer Ark Metals, said customs duties and taxes consume close to 30% of his exploration budget because the emerging industry depends heavily on imported equipment and foreign technical services.  “I really feel bad when I have to raise a hundred dollars and give 30 dollars to the government,” Vohra said.  Rather than seeking permanent exemptions, he proposes deferring those obligations until commercial production begins, allowing companies to invest more capital in exploration while preserving the government’s eventual tax revenue.  “Defer now to prosper tomorrow,” he said.  Aurangzeb acknowledged the industry’s concerns and said the government would consider changes to taxation and other policies, particularly measures supporting exporters. He pointed to the removal of super taxes in this year’s budget.  But he also emphasized Pakistan’s limited fiscal flexibility, warning that a tax-to-GDP ratio below 10% would be unsustainable. The country has only recently moved into double digits.  That creates a policy dilemma. Export-oriented tax relief provides little immediate benefit to explorers that may spend years defining deposits before generating revenue.  Deferral could bridge that gap without permanently eliminating government receipts, although it would postpone collections and leave the treasury exposed if projects never reach production.  Current incentives nevertheless favour processing.  At the forum, Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz Sharif announced the province’s first dedicated mineral processing zone at an industrial estate in Khushab, offering industrial land at nominal rent for 15 years alongside customs duty concessions.  Federal relief for explorers, including a reported 30-year sales tax exemption covering exploration and development, remains under consideration.  The contrast is striking: processing investors are receiving concrete incentives while explorers are still seeking comparable support.  Government officials appear increasingly aware of the sequencing challenge. Barnes said discussions at the forum showed that policymakers had carefully examined the conditions necessary to make domestic smelting commercially viable.  “They understand that until there’s a mining industry here, smelting is not really on the table,” he said. “If they get two, three, four mines that are producing, options start to open up for them.”  Pakistan does not need to abandon its processing ambitions. It needs to distinguish between commodities where domestic refining addresses a genuine supply-chain shortage and copper, where existing smelters are already competing for scarce material.  The immediate priority is to make exploration more attractive, establish dependable production and build an export industry capable of financing future downstream investment.  A domestic copper smelter may eventually make sense. Its economic justification will be stronger once Pakistan has several producing mines and the concentrate supply to sustain it.  For now, the furnace can wait for the rock.  * Erik Groves is a contributing analyst for MINING.COM and Corporate Strategy and In-House Counsel at Morgan Companies. He will attend and provide coverage of the Pakistan Minerals Investment Forum (PMIF) in Islamabad on November 12 and 13. title: Trump, Xi agreed that military AI decisions should involve humans, Bessent says
